name: Everhour
tagline: Time tracking, estimates, budgets, expenses, and invoices for project tools

pricing.notes: Working normalization from the official public pricing structure. Recheck the source page immediately before publication.

tiers.name: Free
tiers.limits: Up to 5 users; time tracking, projects, tasks, reports, and export; 0 project-management integrations

tiers.name: Team
tiers.limits: Minimum 5 paid seats; unlimited seats; integrations, estimates, budgets, expenses, invoicing, and SSO

tiers.name: Custom
tiers.limits: For 50+ users; custom commercial and support terms

pricing.freeTierCaps: 5 users; time tracking, projects, tasks, reports, and export; 0 integrations
pricing.billingTerms: monthly + annual (annual rate is 15% lower); 14-day Team trial
pricing.hiddenCosts: Team has a 5-seat minimum, making the minimum bill $50/month or $42.50/month at the annual rate. Purchased seat count is not automatically reduced when a user is removed; annual unused time is non-refundable.

verdictSummary: Everhour's solo core is compact: build a private time + budget tracking ledger that imports user-supplied CSV files, categorizes entries, reconciles balances, and exports reports. A competent builder can reach a useful personal version in one sitting, while the paid product mainly wins on banking, compliance, trust.
coreLoopDIY: Track hours against clients and projects, compare them to the estimate, and turn the unbilled ones into an invoice line.
replacementScope: personal replacement for the core loop
requirements: CSV exports from the user's own accounts
whatYouLose: integrations with Asana, Trello, Jira and Basecamp, which is what Everhour is for
a team tracking against the same projects, with approvals
invoicing and payment collection at the end of the chain
whyPeopleStillPay: Everhour: people pay because it lives inside the project tool the team already uses, so the hours land next to the work without anyone opening a second app.
ongoingBurden: Own data integrity, backups, import mapping, reconciliation, security, audit logs, tax changes, and recovery.

prompt:
Build me a personal time tracker with project budgets, to replace Everhour.
Use exactly this stack: Node 22 + better-sqlite3 + server-rendered HTML with a little vanilla JS; no build step and no alternative stacks.
Primary job: start and stop a timer against a client and a project, watch the estimate burn down, and turn unbilled hours into an invoice draft.
Start from an empty folder and create the complete working project.
Clients, projects and tasks. A project carries an estimate in hours or money and an hourly rate.
One big start and stop control. Only one timer runs at a time, a running timer survives a restart, and the tab title shows the elapsed time.
Manual entries and edits, where an edit keeps the previous value with a timestamp and a reason. An edit history is the difference between a record and a guess.
A week grid: days across, projects down, totals on both edges, editable in place.
Budget burn-down per project: estimated, tracked, remaining, and the date the estimate runs out at the current pace. Warn at 80 and at 100 percent.
The rate is copied onto the entry when it is booked, so changing a rate later never rewrites what past work was worth.
Turn unbilled entries into an invoice draft grouped by project, and mark them billed only once the draft is saved.
Reports filtered by client, project and date range, exportable as CSV, plus a printable monthly timesheet.
Do not add accounts, telemetry, or a hosted service. Secrets, if any, go in .env.
Include clear empty, loading, success and recoverable error states.
Write focused tests for the timer state machine and for the burn-down arithmetic.
Create a README with setup, where the database lives, and how to back it up.
Deliberately out of scope: integrations with Asana, Trello and Jira, which are the actual reason people pay for Everhour · multi-user approval flows · and sending or collecting payment.
Run the tests and build before finishing, then fix errors rather than describing them.
